title: Fidelity SIPP (CAS-71272-L7B1)
text:
CAS-71272-L7B1
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mr M
Scheme Fidelity SIPP (the SIPP)
Respondent Fidelity International (Fidelity)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Mr M’s complaint is that Fidelity arranged the sale of all the SIPP’s investments on
receipt of the instruction of one of the beneficiaries of the death benefits, for the
withdrawal of their death benefit lump sum. Mr M had been informed only the required
proportion of the investments would be sold. He had intended to keep his share of the
death benefits invested for a longer period and says he has incurred financial loss.
Background information, including submissions from the parties
The sequence of events is not in dispute, so I have only set out the main points. I
acknowledge there were other exchanges of information between all the parties.
In 2015, Mr M’s wife opened the SIPP and provided an Expression of Wish (EOW) to
Fidelity. This said that in the event of her death, Mr M should receive 50% of the
value of the SIPP and the remainder should be split in equal shares (i.e. 25% each)
between their daughter and son.
Section 9.4 of the SIPP terms and conditions (the SIPP Terms) regarding
“Investment” stated:
“In the event of your death any investments will continue to be held until a
payment(s) has been made under the Discretionary Trust. During this time,
however long this may be, the value of investments may fluctuate and we will
not be liable for any loss in the value of your Account(s) due to a fall in the
value of the investments between the date of your death and the date of the
(final) payment.”
1
Fidelity International

CAS-71272-L7B1
Under Clause 1 the SIPP Terms explained “Discretionary Trust means the basis
under which lump sum death benefits are paid out by us. We’ll decide who should
receive such a lump sum, and how much, from the list of beneficiaries described in
the Rules.”
On 11 March 2020, Mr M telephoned Fidelity to advise that his wife had died. She
was under the age of 75 when she died.
On 8 April 2020, Mr M telephoned Fidelity further. This followed its request for
certified copies of the documents it required to process the death benefits. Fidelity
has provided a transcript summarising this conversation which in part confirms Mr M
queried the position of the SIPP. He was informed that “everything stays invested.”
On 12 May 2020, Mr M issued another letter to Fidelity. This enclosed the necessary
documents Fidelity had requested from him over the preceding period, including the
Will. The Will confirmed Mr M as the sole Executor and Trustee.
On 1 June 2020, Mr M telephoned Fidelity to enquire about its progress. Fidelity’s
transcript of this conversation says, “Mr M wanted to check the fund would move in
his name and would continue to be invested” and was informed “we’d 100% definitely
keep it invested.”
On 9 July 2020, Fidelity made the decision that the benefits of the SIPP should be
allocated in accordance with the EOW, that was 50% to Mr M and 25% to each of the
two children.
On 16 July 2020, Fidelity issued a letter to Mr M (the Options Letter). This confirmed
the percentage shares of the death benefits allocated to each beneficiary and their
options in terms of how they could request to receive them. The letter stated there
were three options available to choose from and that a combination of them was
possible. The options were as set out below: -
• “Take the full amount as a tax-free lump sum. Please be aware that this is
subject to a lifetime allowance test and any amount paid above the lifetime
allowance will be subject to a tax charge of 55%” (Option One).
• “Take flexi-access income drawdown while leaving the lump sum invested”
(Option Two).
• “Use the amount to purchase an annuity.”
The Options Letter confirmed the value of the SIPP on 16 July 2020 was
£173,186.91. It also included a request for documents for identity and verification
purposes.
2

CAS-71272-L7B1
The Options Letter also stated “We strongly recommend that before making any
decision you discuss the options and implications with the beneficiary, especially if
they are considering income drawdown. When they have decided how they would like
to take the benefits, please ask them to confirm in writing to the address above”.
Mr M has provided a copy of a separate letter issued to him by Fidelity on 23 July
2020 (the July 2020 Letter). This was notification of a change in the date of the
collection of its service fee. The letter did however also reference the position of the
death claim, where it stated:
“A reminder of your options
If the deceased holdings are still under estate administration, then they’ll
remain invested with us until the executor forwards us the necessary
documentation to close any accounts.
If we’ve received all relevant documents from the executor for registration, and
the assets with Fidelity have already been disbursed, we’ll still need signed
instructions from the executors to transfer or redeem any residual monies
remaining following investments from distributions or suspended funds should
they reopen for trading.
Remember, you have the option to sell into cash should you choose. Where
monies are required to pay for Inheritance Tax or funeral expenses you can
request this by sending us a completed Declaration and Indemnity form. We
can release monies from the deceased’s account directly to HM Revenue &
Customs or the funeral director on your behalf”
On 24 July 2020, Mr M telephoned Fidelity. The transcript of this discussion stated Mr
M was informed the Options Letter had been issued, but he had not received it.
Fidelity explained to Mr M that the beneficiaries had two years to decide what to do.
This was in relation to the fact that tax charges normally become applicable where a
pension member dies under the age of 75 and death benefits are paid or designated
for drawdown more than two years after the pension provider is notified of death.
Mr M asked about the liquidation of the investments and whether it was necessary to
“sell all funds for Option One”. He was informed that “each of them could make their
own decisions and that taking tax free cash would be to withdraw it so it would be
sold.” On the same day, the Options Letter was re-issued to Mr M.
3

CAS-71272-L7B1
On 7 August 2020, Mr M telephoned Fidelity (the August conversation). Mr M
asked if all investments would have to be sold if all beneficiaries chose Option One or
if they could “stay invested”. He was advised they can “transfer to a drawdown
account” or “ask us to sell it and we’d send to their bank accounts”.
The question of tax arose, and Mr M was informed that if the beneficiaries opted for
Option Two, any withdrawals would be taxable. He was informed this option did not
have to be taken immediately and that the lump sum would be paid tax free. The
transcript of this conversation also said that Mr M “wanted the funds to stay the same
for the 2 years”. Further, that Mr M queried how the SIPP would be divided if one
lump sum was paid and was informed that “the fund would be divided proportionately
across the account.”
On 21 August 2020, during a further telephone conversation Fidelity confirmed to
Mr M that the required identity documents could be issued by him separately and
ahead of the beneficiaries providing instructions for the payment of benefits. It was
explained that his children could request Option One individually and that the “others
can wait”. The two-year time limit was also explained.
On 1 September 2020, Mr M issued a letter to Fidelity enclosing the additional
documents requested in the Options Letter. The letter also contained the following
relevant comments from Mr M:
“We have still not decided when we will take the lump sum. The children and I
need more time to decide on when to take the lump sum and I believe we
have two years…” and “Please allow the funds to continue invested in their
existing status.”
On 7 September 2020, Mr M telephoned Fidelity. He queried how his son could take
his lump sum and was “previously told each of them could do what they liked and
whenever they liked” and that Fidelity required a letter of instruction and bank details.
The notes from this conversation show Mr M raised a question about how the funds
to pay his son’s lump sum would be paid and that he was informed his share (of 25%)
would be liquidated “across the board” rather than one fund. It was confirmed to him
that “the rest of the money would remain invested.”
On the same day, Mr M’s son issued an instruction to Fidelity to request the payment
of his full share of the SIPP.
4

CAS-71272-L7B1
On 16 September 2020, Mr M telephoned Fidelity. He was informed that instructions
to sell all investments held in the SIPP had been issued and that the information
provided to him previously, that only part of the SIPP’s investments would be sold if
one beneficiary requested payment, was not correct. Mr M explained his concerns at
this time and his comments were registered as a complaint.
During this conversation, Mr M stated he wanted the account reinvested. He
telephoned Fidelity again on 17 September 2020 and reiterated his concerns. Fidelity
agreed to contact Mr M to let him know if the SIPP funds could be reinvested.
Fidelity has not provided the details of any communication sent to Mr M in this period
in response to his question about reinvesting the cash. However, it has confirmed that
it would not have been possible for it to reinvest funds held in a SIPP where the
original SIPP member had died. It explained that it would only have been possible to
reinvest the funds if the income drawdown option had been selected and a new
beneficiary SIPP had been opened, and money transferred to it and reinvested.
On 27 September 2020, Mr M and his daughter each issued an instruction to Fidelity
to request Option One. Mr M’s letter of instruction explained his concerns and said
that he had incurred financial loss through the total SIPP value dropping from
£182,351 to £174,399. He said these were the values at the time of his wife’s death
and then following the SIPP’s liquidation.
On 28 September 2020, Mr M telephoned Fidelity and expressed his concerns about
the time taken to issue monies to his son. That payment was issued on 30 September
2020.
On 14 October 2020, Fidelity issued £87,195.53 to Mr M. On 16 October 2020, Mr M
contacted Fidelity to further question the time taken to issue monies and he raised a
complaint.
On 20 October 2020, Fidelity sent a letter to Mr M which stated the final value of the
SIPP was £174,440.69 (with £87,195.53 paid to him and £43,622.58 paid to both his
daughter and son).
5

CAS-71272-L7B1
On 3 November 2020, Fidelity issued its response to Mr M’s complaints. Its position is
summarised later in this Determination.
On 16 November 2020, Mr M discussed the matter with Fidelity. He was unhappy it
did not agree to consider his claim for financial loss. A new complaint was registered.
On 21 December 2020, Fidelity issued its further response to Mr M’s complaints. It
reiterated its position and explained that while it did not dispute Mr M was mis-
informed, it was not possible to establish whether any financial loss had been
incurred. It did not agree to meet his claim for financial loss.
On 23 February 2021, Fidelity issued a further letter in reply to Mr M’s complaints to
confirm that its position had not changed.
Summary of Mr M’s position
• He was informed on multiple occasions that each beneficiary could instruct the
withdrawal of their share independently and that in between each instruction the
SIPP investments would remain invested. The whole SIPP was conversely fully
disinvested upon receipt of his son’s instruction and Fidelity actioned this without
his or his daughter’s permission. It should have sought such permission.
• The July 2020 Letter said no action would be taken without the Executor’s
instruction and Fidelity’s position in response to his complaint contradicts this. The
instruction from his son was not valid, since he was the Executor and he was not
notified. Fidelity had a legal obligation to notify him.
• His son’s instruction would not have been issued, had the correct information
been provided to him. His son did not require the funds and as a family they did
not require the monies either. The intention was to keep the SIPP invested until a
time that the value increased and within the relevant two-year period. He made
this clear to Fidelity.
• To resolve his complaint, he wanted all funds reinstated but was told that was not
possible. He did not recall receipt of the Options Letter. He did however discuss
Option Two with Fidelity and was informed any monies drawn that way would be
taxable. The lump sum option was tax free and so, he took this option and so did
his daughter.
• His lump sum had been placed in a savings account in the interim. He explained
that any investment strategy was not at the forefront of his thoughts. He was
bereaved and the death of his wife was very traumatic. His son had used around
£10,000 to clear his student loan. The remainder of his was in a savings account
and a small amount invested in stocks.
6

CAS-71272-L7B1
• Mr M did not need the money. He was a higher rate taxpayer and intended to
leave funds in the more tax-efficient SIPP. That benefit was lost. He was well
aware of the two-year time limit and would have been actively looking for an
appropriate time to encash before the deadline.
• He did not agree with Fidelity’s view that financial loss could not be quantified. It
was clear that the markets had improved as of 22 February 2022, which was two
years on from the date his wife had died. He estimated his financial loss was
about £9,000, on the assumption 75% of the SIPP would have remained invested
for the majority of the two-year period. In his submissions to The Pensions
Ombudsman (TPO) he explained that figure was based on “present day value.”
Summary of Fidelity’s position
• It accepted that Mr M was mis-informed and his lump sum payment was delayed,
so it upheld his complaints. The misinformation was however an error in
communication rather than a reflection of the actual process or options available.
• Its normal process for the distribution of death benefits where there are multiple
beneficiaries was to liquidate the entire SIPP upon receipt of the first instruction.
This was to protect against market fluctuations and to ensure each beneficiary
receives the correct share of monies.
• It was correct and in accordance with its standard procedure for it to act on the
instruction received from Mr M’s son, as this was a valid and confirmed instruction
from a beneficiary. The instruction superseded and contradicted the earlier
indication provided by Mr M, that none of the beneficiaries would be taking the
lump sum until later.
• There was no evidence to support Mr M’s claim that his son would not have
issued his instructions for his lump sum. It said that this instruction necessitated
the full liquidation of the SIPP, to ensure each beneficiary received the correct
percentage of the fund, without the risk of market fluctuations.
• It could not reinvest into a SIPP where the SIPP member had died, and the sales
of the SIPP’s investments were irreversible. Further, it was not possible to
establish with any certainty when disinvestments may have occurred (if the actual
sales did not occur) and if they were placed later, whether the lump sums received
would have been higher or not. So, it was not possible to establish if any financial
loss had been incurred.
7

CAS-71272-L7B1
• The Options Letter issued to Mr M included application forms that would have
allowed him and his daughter to open their own beneficiary SIPP accounts and to
reinvest the cash. These forms were not completed and returned before the lump
sum payment to Mr M’s son was processed.
• During the August Conversation, its agent did not consider and explain to Mr M
that if he selected Option Two and if funds were designated within two years,
income payments would not be taxable. It explained that the agent instead
referred to what it said was the default position, where income is taxable and that
was confirmed to Mr M. Fidelity said its agent should have been clearer and it
apologised.
• It would normally issue a withdrawal where funds are already in cash in 8 working
days and the lump sum payments made to Mr M and his daughter were made 6
working days late. So, it accepted it caused a delay.
• It made an offer to pay Mr M interest of £24.46 and his daughter £12.24 in relation
to the late payments. £500 was offered to Mr M for non-financial injustice. It felt
those offers were fair in the circumstances.
Adjudicator’s Opinion
8

CAS-71272-L7B1
9

CAS-71272-L7B1
Fidelity accepted the Adjudicator’s Opinion and did not provide any other comments.
Mr M did not accept the Opinion, and he provided his additional comments, which are
summarised below.
• The Opinion was based on the SIPP Terms and ignored the issue of incorrect
information. The decision did not explain how Fidelity could justify the wrong
information it provided and not take responsibility for it. It was the wrong
information alone that led to his son instructing the payment of his lump sum.
• The Adjudicator did not question whether his son would have issued his
instruction if he had known all the SIPP’s investments would be sold. It was wrong
to conclude that his son’s instruction would have been issued anyway.
• The Opinion “downplayed” his role as the sole Executor and beneficiary of his
wife’s Will. He expected the findings to recognise that Fidelity failed to notify him
before selling the whole SIPP. Its letter said it would not do so unless it received
instructions from all beneficiaries.
• He did not agree with the Adjudicator’s view that he had not incurred any financial
loss. He had provided evidence to show he intended to stay invested for the
relevant two-year period.
As Mr M did not accept the Adjudicator’s Opinion, the complaint was passed to me to
consider. I have considered the post Opinion comments provided by Mr M, but they
do not change the outcome. I agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion.
Ombudsman’s decision
Mr M complained that Fidelity sold all the SIPP’s investments on its receipt of his
son’s instruction for the payment of his lump sum. He contends Fidelity should not
have done so without his permission. He had made clear to it he intended to keep his
share of the SIPP invested, and he was the Executor of his late wife’s Will.
Fidelity accepted it provided Mr M with wrong information when it informed him only
the required proportion of the SIPP’s investment would be sold, if only one of the
beneficiaries requested their lump sum. It has explained its normal policy where there
are multiple beneficiaries, is to liquidate all investments after the first instruction is
received.
10

CAS-71272-L7B1
I agree with the Adjudicator’s view that the provision of incorrect information by
Fidelity amounts to maladministration. However, I reiterate what the Adjudicator
added to this point, which is that this fact alone does not necessarily lead me to the
conclusion that Mr M’s complaint should be upheld and his claim for financial loss
should be met.
I must consider the entire circumstances of the complaint as a whole and pertinently,
whether Fidelity acted in a way that I would expect any reasonable SIPP
Administrator or Trustee to act.
After Mr M’s wife died, the SIPP’s investments were held by Fidelity for it to pay out
the death benefits. My general expectation is that death benefits should be allocated
and paid to all beneficiaries as soon as possible. That is once all beneficiaries have
been identified and sufficient time has been allowed to obtain all relevant information
and instructions. It may also depend on the liquidity of the investments held, which I
note was not an issue in this case.
I consider that the liquidation of all investments at the same time and at an earlier
stage is an appropriate and logical approach to take. That might be upon receipt of
notification of death, or as in this case, after receipt of the first beneficiary instruction.
This approach is logical because it enables the correct distribution of benefits in the
correct proportions and it protects against possible negative market fluctuations.
I have also reviewed the SIPP Terms. I agree with the Adjudicator’s comments, that
they did not prevent Fidelity from arranging the sale of all the SIPP’s investments on
receipt of the instruction from Mr M’s son. Its primary obligation was to pay the death
benefits under the Discretionary Trust, and it was necessary for Fidelity to act on that
instruction.
I would not expect any reasonable SIPP Administrator or Trustee’s standard position
to typically allow for a late member’s SIPP’s investments to stay invested in the
original SIPP for a longer period, unless there was a valid reason. I consider it would
be unusual for investments to remain as they were purely for the reason of potential
future investment return.
That was the reason why Mr M has said he wanted to delay his instructions for his
lump sum; he was looking for the SIPP’s investments to increase in value. He also
said he did not require any funds at the time of the events that are the subject of his
complaint. In my view, the more appropriate option for him in the circumstances
would have been to apply to Fidelity for the opening of a new beneficiary SIPP in his
own name – an option that was confirmed to him by Fidelity (Option Two). Further, if
he was unsure about what he should do, he could reasonably have obtained
independent financial advice.
11

CAS-71272-L7B1
In conclusion, I find that given the circumstances it was not unreasonable for Fidelity
to have liquidated all the SIPP’s investments when it did. Such action was in
accordance with how I would expect any reasonable SIPP Administrator or Trustee to
act and it follows that I do not consider maladministration has occurred, in relation to
the liquidation of the SIPP.
Mr M has said that Fidelity should have contacted him before acting on any
instructions, given that he was the Executor of his wife’s Will and the July 2020 Letter
said it would do so. The investments were held by Fidelity until it liquidated them to
make payment under the Discretionary Trust, and I find there was no requirement for
it to notify Mr M before liquidation occurred.
I have said that maladministration did occur in terms of the wrong information
provided to Mr M by Fidelity. While it is disappointing that wrong information was
provided, I agree with the Adjudicator’s findings on this point. My general position on
a complaint of negligent misstatement is that there must have been loss suffered in
consequence of the misstatement being reasonably relied on. Reasonable reliance
requires reliance on the misstatement but also showing that they would have acted
differently if the incorrect information had not been. The loss must be a consequence
of the reliance and not too remote or something the person could have avoided or
that resulted from action by a third party.
In this case, I find that the disinvestment was a consequence of Fidelity’s policies and
of Mr M’s son requesting payment of his lump sum. The sense in which Mr M asserts
reliance on the incorrect statement is that his son did not defer requesting payment of
his portion to allow Mr M to accrue potential investment returns. I appreciate that Mr
M has stated that his son would have deferred requesting his lump sum had Mr M not
been told that his portion of the SIPP would remain invested after a request for
payment by any of the other beneficiaries. However, I cannot find reasonable reliance
in a failure to procure another person, his son, defer accessing his benefit when it
was in his son’s interest to access it, given that he has used it to invest and pay off a
student loan. I could not direct Fidelity to put Mr M in the position he would have been
in if his son had not accessed his own lump sum.
I also find that Mr M had the option to reinvest his portion by using Option Two and
would have suffered no loss of investment return had he chosen that option. In other
words, he had an option to mitigate any loss of investment return.
12

CAS-71272-L7B1
My awards for non-financial injustice will generally fall into one of the following five
categories: nominal, significant, serious, severe and exceptional. The amounts range
from nil where I consider distress and inconvenience to be nominal to £2,000 where I
consider it to be severe, or more only where it is considered to be exceptional. I
consider that the distress and inconvenience Mr M has experienced falls into the
significant category. So, I find the existing offer of £500 to be appropriate.
I do not uphold Mr M’s complaint.
Camilla Barry
Deputy Pensions Ombudsman
14 July 2026
13
